metaDescription: Five snow blowers under $1000, from a two-stage gas machine to premium cordless units, compared on power, width and what the extra money buys.
expertTake: The BILT HARD 24-inch two-stage gas machine is the pick for deep, heavy snow because it is the only true two-stage design here. The EGO SNT2122 is the best cordless choice if you already live inside the EGO battery system. Skip the whole group if your driveway is small and flat, because a cheaper single-stage electric machine will do the same work.
introParagraphs: This price band is where the choice splits in two. You can step up to a gas two-stage machine that handles deep, wet snow, or you can pay for a premium cordless single-stage unit that is quieter and needs far less upkeep.

The right answer depends on the snow you actually get, not the budget alone. Prices move and the $1000 cap reflects listing prices when this guide was updated, so check the live number before you buy.

products.name: BILT HARD 24-Inch 212cc Two-Stage Gas Snow Blower
products.description:
This is a real two-stage machine: serrated steel augers break up and pull in the snow, then a separate impeller throws it out of the chute. The 212cc four-stroke OHV engine is rated at 3600 rpm and drives the augers and wheels through a self-propelled system with six forward speeds and two reverse. That combination is what lets it chew through packed plow-ridge snow that would stall any electric single-stage unit in this guide.

The trade is weight and upkeep. Compared with the EGO SNT2122, it is far heavier and you must deal with fuel, oil, a spark plug and a carburetor each season. It also has an electric start for cold mornings, but that only helps if you plug it in to a 120V outlet and keep the battery or cord in order.

Ownership matters more than the spec sheet. Stabilize or drain the fuel before summer, change the oil once a season, and carry spare shear pins. The brand is less established than the major gas-engine names, so confirm warranty and parts availability.
products.bestFor: Long driveways and regions with heavy, wet or drifted snow.
pros: True two-stage design handles deep snow
Electric start helps in cold weather
cons: Needs fuel, oil and seasonal service

products.name: EGO Power+ SNT2122 21-Inch Single-Stage Cordless
products.description:
EGO combines two 56V ARC packs in a Peak Power mode that boosts output under load. A variable-speed auger lets you slow the machine for light snow and speed it up for heavy, and a 180-degree chute helps you aim the throw. The listing says it can clear a ten-car driveway of 8 inches on a charge, which is a best-case claim but shows how much energy two 4Ah packs hold.

Against the BILT HARD it clears fewer inches of deep snow, but it starts instantly and weighs a fraction of the gas unit. Against the Greenworks 80V it has the stronger throw and faster charging thanks to the 320W charger, but costs more for the privilege. If you own EGO mowers or trimmers, the packs are shared.

Year-three ownership is simple: store packs indoors, keep the charger vents clear, and replace the rubber scraper bar when it wears. There is no fuel to go stale and no carburetor to clean.
products.bestFor: Users in the EGO battery system who want gas-like power without fuel.
pros: Peak Power boosts output under heavy load
Variable auger speed matches snow depth
cons: Single-stage cannot match a two-stage on deep snow
High cost for a single-stage unit
Throw drops sharply in wet snow

products.name: SENIX 40V 21-Inch Cordless Snow Blower 1800W
products.description:
SENIX pairs a 21-inch path with a brushless motor rated at 1800W and a steel auger with variable speed. The 12-inch depth rating is the deepest single-pass claim among the battery units here, though depth capability in practice depends on how wet the snow is. Variable speed is a practical feature: you can slow the auger on light snow to save charge.

Compared with the EGO SNT2122, the SENIX gives up Peak Power and ecosystem depth but costs noticeably less. Compared with the WORX WG461, it is a little wider at 21 inches, though the WORX ships with larger 6Ah packs. The brand is newer, so read the warranty carefully and keep the receipt.

Plan on carrying both batteries indoors between storms. The steel auger is tougher than a plastic one, but check the rubber scraper every season and tighten the chute fasteners.
products.bestFor: A wide cordless blower without the premium brand price.
cons: Newer brand with a thin parts network
Throw distance is not the best

products.name: Greenworks 80V 20-Inch Brushless Snow Blower
products.description:
The Greenworks uses the maker's 80V platform, and its brushless motor is designed for quiet operation and low maintenance. The 20-inch clearing path covers driveways, patios and walks in fewer passes than an 18-inch unit. With one 4Ah pack in the box, plan to buy a second if your driveway is long.

It is cheaper than the EGO SNT2122 and has one pack instead of two, so the kit is not equal. Where it earns its place is in ownership: no oil, no gas, and a battery platform that powers mowers and trimmers in the same range.

The usual cold rules apply. Keep the pack inside until you need it, and do not leave it on the charger over summer at full charge.
products.bestFor: Greenworks 80V owners who want a quiet, simple machine.
cons: Only one 4Ah battery in the kit

products.name: WORX WG461 40V 20-Inch Cordless Snow Blower
products.description:
WORX ships this model with two 20V 6Ah PowerShare Pro batteries, so you have 12Ah of capacity in the box. The 20-inch by 10-inch intake and stated 35-foot throw are good for light to moderate snow. Total stored energy in the kit is generous compared with the single-pack Greenworks.

It costs less than the SENIX or EGO machines but has a weaker motor claim. If your priority is runtime per kit rather than top-end torque, it is a solid choice. Packs are shared with the maker's 20V tools.

As with all single-stage units, avoid gravel and take deep snow in layers. Keep spare packs warm and rotate them to even out wear.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want long runtime per kit and a mid-range price.
cons: Lower peak power than EGO or SENIX
Two packs take time to recharge

buyingCriteria.explanation: A two-stage machine has an auger that feeds snow to a separate impeller. The BILT HARD 24-inch is the only one here, and it handles snow deeper than 12 inches and wet drifts. Single-stage units such as the EGO SNT2122 and SENIX scrape pavement and suit up to roughly 8 inches. If your driveway is over about 60 feet or your storms are heavy, choose two-stage.

Gas gives unlimited runtime and the most power, but you take on fuel, oil and carburetor care. Battery machines start instantly and need almost no upkeep, but runtime depends on pack capacity. The EGO SNT2122 with two 4Ah packs and the WORX with two 6Ah packs show how kits differ. Leaving old fuel in the BILT HARD over summer is the most common reason it fails to start.

Buying into EGO, Greenworks 80V or WORX means committing to that maker's battery system. If you already own mowers or trimmers from the same family, extra packs are cheaper because the platform is shared. If you do not, compare the cost of a second pack, since runtime on a large driveway depends on it.

A 24-inch two-stage like the BILT HARD clears more per pass than the 20-inch Greenworks, but it is heavier to turn. A 21-inch machine such as the SENIX or EGO covers most driveways in fewer passes than an 18-inch unit. Match width to the narrowest obstacle you must pass. Before you buy, measure the narrowest gap on your route and the length of the longest straight pass.

Two-stage machines use drive wheels so you steer rather than push. The BILT HARD offers six forward and two reverse speeds. Cordless single-stage units are lighter and rely on the auger to pull them forward. On steep driveways traction matters more than engine size. Test the drive on a ramp if you can: slow, steady traction beats a larger engine on ice.

Gas engines need fresh fuel and proper choke use in cold weather, though electric start helps. Lithium packs lose output near 0 F, so store them indoors until use. Both are easy to fix, but ignoring them is the top cause of a machine that seems underpowered.

specDecoder.meaning: A bigger displacement generally gives more torque, but design and gearing decide real output. 212cc is a common size for a 24-inch two-stage blower.
specDecoder.watchFor: Check the BILT HARD's 212cc rating against its 24-inch width to see it is sized properly.

specDecoder.meaning: A short-duration boost that draws from two packs when the motor is under load. It improves performance in dense snow but drains the packs faster.
specDecoder.watchFor: The EGO SNT2122 advertises it, while the SENIX and WORX do not.

specDecoder.meaning: Battery capacity. Multiply by voltage to compare stored energy between kits.
specDecoder.watchFor: The WORX has two 6Ah packs while the Greenworks has one 4Ah pack.

specDecoder.meaning: The farthest the chute can throw light snow. It falls sharply with wet, heavy snow.
specDecoder.watchFor: The EGO claims up to 42 ft and the WORX up to 35 ft.

specDecoder.meaning: Forward and reverse speeds let you match walking pace to snow depth.
specDecoder.watchFor: The BILT HARD has six forward and two reverse gears.

howWeEvaluated.title: Machine type and depth
howWeEvaluated.description: We separated two-stage from single-stage designs because it decides snow depth capability. The BILT HARD stands alone as two-stage. Single-stage units were compared on intake height. This matters because buyers often assume more money always means more depth capability, when only the machine architecture changes that.

howWeEvaluated.title: Power source
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared gas and battery in terms of upkeep, runtime and start-up. Kits with two packs were judged against single-pack kits. The EGO and WORX kits were the main reference points. This keeps a cheap-looking kit from hiding the cost of a second battery.

howWeEvaluated.title: Width and handling
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at clearing width against likely driveway size. Wider machines clear faster but are harder to turn. The 24-inch BILT HARD and 20-inch Greenworks bracket the range. Narrow gates, parked cars and planters decide the practical limit more often than the spec sheet does.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ownership cost
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered what you must buy and maintain after purchase. Extra batteries, fuel, oil and spark plugs all add up. Cordless units have lower routine costs. A machine that costs less to run can beat a slightly stronger one over five winters.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value within the cap
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at which features you get for a price near the cap. Peak Power, variable-speed augers and two-pack kits were the main differences. The SENIX and WORX offer value without a premium brand. We weighted these differences more than brand reputation.

rows: Peak Power with variable auger speed
Two 6Ah packs at a modest cost

cards.label: Gas
cards.text: The BILT HARD gives unlimited runtime and handles deep snow. It needs fuel, oil and seasonal service, and it is heavy to store.

cards.label: Battery
cards.text: The EGO SNT2122, SENIX, Greenworks and WORX start instantly and need almost no service. Their runtime is limited by pack capacity, and they are weaker in deep wet snow.

howToChoose.note: Choose gas for heavy snow and long drives; choose battery for moderate snow and low upkeep.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A 21 to 24 inch path, enough battery capacity for a full pass, or a gas engine for unlimited runtime.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The BILT HARD handles the largest areas and deepest snow. The EGO SNT2122 is the best battery option, and the SENIX adds a wide path at a lower price.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You face heavy snow or a long drive. Step up to the BILT HARD two-stage, or to the EGO SNT2122 for premium cordless power and a faster charger.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Your driveway is short and storms are light. The WORX WG461 or Greenworks 80V will do the job at lower cost.

maintenance.why: Cold starts wash oil thin. Fresh oil protects the engine through the winter.
Old fuel gums carburetors. Draining it or adding stabilizer prevents hard starts.
Cold reduces output and shortens lifespan. Keep packs at partial charge and dry.
Worn parts reduce clearing. Carry spare shear pins for a quick swap.
Vibration loosens bolts. Tightening avoids breakage.

faq.a: If you get more than 10 inches of snow or have a long driveway, yes. The BILT HARD in this guide is two-stage, while the others are single-stage. Before the first big storm, run the machine once on dry pavement to confirm the auger spins freely and the chute turns, and charge every pack or check the oil. Never clear a jam by hand: stop the engine or remove the battery first, then use a stick or the supplied clearing tool.

faq.q: Can a cordless unit replace a gas blower?
faq.a: For moderate snow on a paved driveway, yes. For deep, wet or drifted snow, a gas two-stage still has the advantage.

faq.q: How long do the batteries last?
faq.a: Runtime depends on pack capacity and snow type. Two-pack kits such as the EGO SNT2122 and WORX WG461 give the longest working time. Pick EGO if you already use its batteries elsewhere or want the strongest throw and fastest charger; the SENIX or WORX suit those who only want a snow tool at the lowest kit cost.

faq.q: Does a higher voltage mean more power?
faq.a: Not alone. Compare voltage multiplied by amp-hours and consider the motor design.

faq.q: Can I use a single-stage on gravel?
faq.a: Not safely. The auger touches the surface and throws stones. Use a two-stage with adjustable skid shoes.
Drain or stabilize fuel for gas machines, and store battery packs indoors at partial charge.
